power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Humans are highly social, and much of that sociality is regulatory.
Individuals do not manage the demands placed upon their mind and body alone but through and with others.
Attachment science has pursued how the brain accomplishes this regulation for the better part of a century, and its most recent contribution has been neurobiological.

Within the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we previously specified a neuroanatomical architecture of two interacting systems and four domain general modules for organised attachment, extended it to attachment disruption and disorganisation, and moved it from single brains to dyads within Relational Neuroscience, which builds on second-person neuroscience and uses hyperscanning as its principal method.
What that work established energetically, through social allostasis, it did not specify computationally.
Here, we close that gap.

Drawing on active inference, allostasis as interoceptive inference, and recent constructs of attachment as prediction, we propose the term social allostatic inference: the attachment system as one predictive-allostatic loop, the four modules as its functional components, and organised, disrupted, and disorganised attachment as characteristic settings of the precision parameters that govern it.

We extend our account to the caregiving system, which we propose, as a testable extension, to share this architecture while inferring the state it regulates from exteroceptive evidence about another body rather than from interoceptive evidence about its own.
At the level of the dyad, interpersonal neural and biobehavioural synchrony are read, as a hypothesis, as indices of where regulatory work is invested rather than of bond quality directly.
We state the generative model that our account presupposes, specify observations that would count against it, and set out a measurement programme.
Humans are highly social, and much of that sociality is regulatory.
Individuals do not manage the demands placed upon their bodies alone but through and with others.

How the brain accomplishes this regulation, and why individuals differ so markedly in their capacity and motivation to perform it, is the question that attachment science has pursued for the better part of a century.
The most recent contribution to that integration has been the investigation of the neurobiology underlying attachment.

It proceeded first through non-human animal models of pair bonding and parental care and then through the study of humans, where neurobiological measurement initially served to corroborate hypotheses of attachment theory that behavioural methods alone could not adjudicate (Gustison & Phelps, 2022).
text.formatted: It proceeded first through non-human animal models of pair bonding and parental care and then through the study of humans, where neurobiological measurement initially served to corroborate hypotheses of attachment theory that behavioural methods alone could not adjudicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Gustison & Phelps, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The human-directed line of enquiry has since become an identifiable programme that we have termed the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment, or SoNeAt (White et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The human-directed line of enquiry has since become an identifiable programme that we have termed the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment, or SoNeAt <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">(White et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our own contribution to SoNeAt has been cumulative, and it is better characterised by what it collectively established than by the order in which its parts appeared.
Across that work, we have made five overarching commitments, which the present manuscript takes as its foundation.
The first commitment is architectural.

We began from the observation that the social neuroscience literature could be organised along attachment-theoretical lines, although large parts of it have been collected without attachment in mind (Vrticka & Vuilleumier, 2012).
text.formatted: We began from the observation that the social neuroscience literature could be organised along attachment-theoretical lines, although large parts of it have been collected without attachment in mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">(Vrticka & Vuilleumier, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, we proposed that the neural substrates recruited in attachment-relevant situations are best described as two interacting systems, an affective evaluation system and a cognitive control system, decomposed into four modules: aversion and approach on the affective side, and emotion regulation and mental state representation on the cognitive side (Long et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Accordingly, we proposed that the neural substrates recruited in attachment-relevant situations are best described as two interacting systems, an affective evaluation system and a cognitive control system, decomposed into four modules: aversion and approach on the affective side, and emotion regulation and mental state representation on the cognitive side <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Long et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: None of the four modules is specific to attachment, and there is neither a dedicated attachment area nor a dedicated attachment system.

Each module corresponds approximately to a domaingeneral large-scale network (see also Figure 1), and attachment-related variation is variation in the parameters of shared machinery rather than in its identity (White et al., 2023), as we will further develop below.
text.formatted: Each module corresponds approximately to a domaingeneral large-scale network (see also Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>), and attachment-related variation is variation in the parameters of shared machinery rather than in its identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">(White et al., 2023)</ref>, as we will further develop below.

text.text: The second commitment is sequential.
Onto this architecture, we mapped a prototypical initial attachment pathway, i.e., the most likely ordered sequence of processes elicited when the attachment system is activated (see also Figure 1).
text.formatted: Onto this architecture, we mapped a prototypical initial attachment pathway, i.e., the most likely ordered sequence of processes elicited when the attachment system is activated (see also Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: It runs from the appraisal of threat, through proximity seeking and co-regulation, to the alleviation of distress and the deactivation of the system, together with the derivatives of that sequence associated with organised attachment security, avoidance, and anxiety.
(M. Long et al., 2020).
text.formatted: (M. <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Long et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Having specified this architecture and sequence for organised attachment, we subsequently extended the same account to the disruption and disorganisation of attachment (White et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Having specified this architecture and sequence for organised attachment, we subsequently extended the same account to the disruption and disorganisation of attachment <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">(White et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This extension characterised the divergent regulatory profiles that follow when the caregiving environment fails more severely than the organised insecure strategies can compensate for, distinguishing two routes by their caregiving origin.
On the first, associated with maltreatment, the caregiver is present but is itself a source of threat, which we linked to a hyper-arousal neurophysiological phenotype.

On the second, associated with neglect, the caregiver is instead absent, and it is that absence, and the distress it leaves unassuaged, that constitutes the threat, which we linked to a hypo-arousal phenotype.
The third commitment is to fine-grained neurobiological description.

Where the architecture and the pathway operate at the level of modules and networks, we subsequently specified the cascade of neurobiological events that accompanies attachment behaviour at the level of circuits and signalling systems: from thalamic and amygdalar threat processing through noradrenergic and dopaminergic mobilisation, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) recruitment, and oxytocinergic and opioidergic modulation at reunion, to the consolidation of the episode in memory (Izaki et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Where the architecture and the pathway operate at the level of modules and networks, we subsequently specified the cascade of neurobiological events that accompanies attachment behaviour at the level of circuits and signalling systems: from thalamic and amygdalar threat processing through noradrenergic and dopaminergic mobilisation, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) recruitment, and oxytocinergic and opioidergic modulation at reunion, to the consolidation of the episode in memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Izaki et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The fourth commitment is extending.

We moved the SoNeAt account from data assessed in one participant at a time and thus concerned with the isolated brain, to the simultaneous acquisition of brain activity in dyads assessed during direct interaction.

This step followed second-person neuroscience, which pioneered the notion that social cognition differs fundamentally when individuals interact with rather than merely observe one another (Schilbach et al., 2013; Redcay & Schilbach, 2019), and which was later given Bayesian and active inference formulations (Bolis et al., 2017; Lehmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This step followed second-person neuroscience, which pioneered the notion that social cognition differs fundamentally when individuals interact with rather than merely observe one another <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">(Schilbach et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Redcay & Schilbach, 2019)</ref>, and which was later given Bayesian and active inference formulations <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Bolis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Lehmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In doing so, we incorporated biobehavioural synchrony (BBS) and interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) within what we have more recently called Relational Neuroscience, which builds on the second-person neuroscience tradition and uses hyperscanning as its principal method (De Felice et al., 2025; Long et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In doing so, we incorporated biobehavioural synchrony (BBS) and interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) within what we have more recently called Relational Neuroscience, which builds on the second-person neuroscience tradition and uses hyperscanning as its principal method <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(De Felice et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Long et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: And we emphasised co-regulation and mutual prediction as candidate neurobiological correlates of attachment.
The fifth commitment is to integration.
We asked whether an overarching neurobiological account of human attachment begins to emerge when SoNeAt evidence is combined with adjacent social neuroscience theory.
We argued that it does, by linking attachment to fundamental processes of energy conservation and co-regulation through social allostasis (White et al., 2023).
text.formatted: We argued that it does, by linking attachment to fundamental processes of energy conservation and co-regulation through social allostasis <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">(White et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: When making this integrative suggestion, however, we did not supply a specification of the computations by which the brain accomplishes social allostasis in the context of attachment.
In the present manuscript, we advance our contribution to SoNeAt by closing that gap.
Our aim is to specify the computations that underpin social allostasis as part of human attachment interactions.

To do so, we first draw on the recent literature pertaining to the neuroscience of homeostasis, allostasis and active inference, in accordance with the first formulation of infant attachment as a minimisation of free energy (Cittern et al., 2018) and a recent conceptualisation of attachment as prediction (Tottenham & Vannucci, 2025).
text.formatted: To do so, we first draw on the recent literature pertaining to the neuroscience of homeostasis, allostasis and active inference, in accordance with the first formulation of infant attachment as a minimisation of free energy <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Cittern et al., 2018)</ref> and a recent conceptualisation of attachment as prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">(Tottenham & Vannucci, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We then apply these insights to our functional neuroanatomical models of organised (NAMA) and disrupted and disorganised (NAMDA) attachment, and subsequently extend these considerations to the level of dyads.

That extension requires a further step not previously formalised within SoNeAt: the explicit differentiation of the attachment system from the caregiving system as two related but asymmetric loops, the first activated by threat or distress to the self and terminating in the restoration of one's own felt security, the second activated by another's signalled distress and terminating in its alleviation.
We develop the caregiving loop as a testable extension of NAMA rather than as an established architecture.
More generally, our manuscript is a theoretical synthesis and not a systematic review.
It draws on primary and  >Conceptual Groundwork: Social Allostasis, active inference and attachment

text.text: Every organism must keep its body and mind within survivable limits, which requires continual regulation against fluctuating demand.
For a summary of Section 2 vocabulary, please refer to Box 1.
Homeostasis, in the classical sense, is reactive regulation.
Its feedback loops correct a deviation after it has arisen to restore a regulated variable towards its reference value (or range of values) (Sterling, 2012).
text.formatted: Its feedback loops correct a deviation after it has arisen to restore a regulated variable towards its reference value (or range of values) <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Sterling, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Homeostasis' social counterpart applies the same logic to social connection.

On the account of social homeostasis, the brain treats connection as a basic need, and when it falls short, conserved neural systems register the deficit and drive the organism towards restoration (Allsop et al., 2025; Cressy et al., 2026; Matthews & Tye, 2019).
text.formatted: On the account of social homeostasis, the brain treats connection as a basic need, and when it falls short, conserved neural systems register the deficit and drive the organism towards restoration <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Allsop et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Cressy et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Matthews & Tye, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Allostasis extends homeostasis into the predictive domain.
Rather than waiting for deviations to occur, the brain anticipates the demand that will fall on the regulated variable.
By preparing for regulation in advance, future deviations can be reduced in magnitude and frequency.
In doing so, allostasis governs the homeostatic loops, overrides them and, where demand persists, resets the reference values they defend (Sterling, 2012).
text.formatted: In doing so, allostasis governs the homeostatic loops, overrides them and, where demand persists, resets the reference values they defend <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Sterling, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Allostasis' social counterpart, social allostasis, distributes this predictive work across bodies.
The predicted demands, and the resources mobilised to meet them, are shared between more than one organism.
This is co-regulation, the process by which one individual's physiological states are regulated in part through the behaviour and physiology of others (Atzil et al., 2018; Saxbe et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This is co-regulation, the process by which one individual's physiological states are regulated in part through the behaviour and physiology of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Atzil et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Saxbe et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, sustaining both reactive and predictive regulation through homeostasis and allostasis is costly.
Each act of mobilisation and anticipation draws on the body's resources.
When demand is high, mobilisation is chronic and/or the anticipations are repeatedly in error, that cost accumulates rather than dissipating.

Accordingly, at the individual level, allostatic load denotes this cumulative burden, which, as it builds, can come to exceed the organism's capacity to absorb it (McEwen & Stellar, 1993; Theriault et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Accordingly, at the individual level, allostatic load denotes this cumulative burden, which, as it builds, can come to exceed the organism's capacity to absorb it <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(McEwen & Stellar, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">Theriault et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Social allostatic load extends the same logic of wear and tear to the dyad and the group (Saxbe et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Social allostatic load extends the same logic of wear and tear to the dyad and the group <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">(Saxbe et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Two positions supply the rationale for treating attachment in the terms of social allostasis.
First, Social Baseline Theory holds that the human brain assumes proximity to others as its default ecology.

It expresses this assumption in the economics of risk and effort, such that relational partners are incorporated into neural representations of the self, and their presence lowers the metabolic bid required to meet a given goal (Beckes & Coan, 2011; Coan & Sbarra, 2015).
text.formatted: It expresses this assumption in the economics of risk and effort, such that relational partners are incorporated into neural representations of the self, and their presence lowers the metabolic bid required to meet a given goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Beckes & Coan, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Coan & Sbarra, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Second, an Evolutionary Account of Social Regulation proposes that social animals are those that cannot survive alone and depend on conspecifics to regulate their ongoing physiology.
On this account, the human infant is born in a state of allostatic dependency whose external management is the condition under which their brain develops (Atzil et al., 2018).
text.formatted: On this account, the human infant is born in a state of allostatic dependency whose external management is the condition under which their brain develops <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Atzil et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Both positions converge on the operative principle of our SoNeAt account (White et al., 2023), namely that personal and social resources are neurobiologically treated as nearly interchangeable, so that the more an individual can draw upon others' resources through coregulation, the less personal bioenergetic resource is expended.
text.formatted: Both positions converge on the operative principle of our SoNeAt account <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">(White et al., 2023)</ref>, namely that personal and social resources are neurobiologically treated as nearly interchangeable, so that the more an individual can draw upon others' resources through coregulation, the less personal bioenergetic resource is expended.

text.text: This proposition has recently been examined experimentally at the level of homeostatic efficiency.
In preregistered experiments, participants underwent standardised physiological challenges once alone and once in the presence of a close partner.

The time-integrated deviation from baseline, i.e., the incremental area under the curve (for glucose, above a fixed threshold), was found to be lower in the partner condition for glucose regulation after a carbohydrate load, for skin temperature during a cold challenge, and for electrodermal responses to a stressor in adults and in infants (Masalha et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The time-integrated deviation from baseline, i.e., the incremental area under the curve (for glucose, above a fixed threshold), was found to be lower in the partner condition for glucose regulation after a carbohydrate load, for skin temperature during a cold challenge, and for electrodermal responses to a stressor in adults and in infants <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Masalha et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Effects were small within participants and small to moderate between participants, and the adult electrodermal effect reached significance only between participants.

However, the effect on glucose regulation remained after controlling for electrodermal activity and touch, the pooled adult effect remained after controlling for relationship satisfaction, and the authors propose socially informed allostasis as one candidate route.
Attachment and caregiving were not assessed.
Social allostasis specifies what attachment relationships yield energetically, but not the computations by which the brain accomplishes them.
Active inference supplies this specification.
Because the brain has no direct access to the causes of its sensory and interoceptive signals, it must infer them.
It does so by running an internal model that constantly predicts what it expects to sense, and by comparing those predictions against what actually arrives (Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: It does so by running an internal model that constantly predicts what it expects to sense, and by comparing those predictions against what actually arrives <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Three concepts are important within this context.
First, priors are the expectations the generative model holds before new evidence arrives.
They encode what the brain estimates as most probable based on past experience.
Second, prediction error is the residual mismatch between those expectations and the actually received signals.
And third, precision is the confidence, or inverse variance, assigned to a signal versus an expectation.
This balance governs the weight a prediction error is granted in updating the model, such that a highly precise prediction error compels revision whereas an imprecise one is largely discounted.
Yet, precision is not a single quantity, and we use four terms to refer to it (see Box 1).
First, sensory or interoceptive precision is the weight granted to ascending prediction error, whether interoceptive, arising from the body, or exteroceptive, arising from the world.
Second, prior precision is the confidence with which an expectation is held.
Third, volatility is the expected rate at which the environment changes, which sets how readily a prior is revised (Mathys et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Third, volatility is the expected rate at which the environment changes, which sets how readily a prior is revised <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Mathys et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: And finally, policy precision is the confidence with which one course of action is selected over its alternatives (Parr & Friston, 2018; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015).
text.formatted: And finally, policy precision is the confidence with which one course of action is selected over its alternatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">(Parr & Friston, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Schwartenbeck et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the content of a prior, e.g., whether an attachment figure is expected to be available, is distinct from all four.
Given these quantities, the system can reduce prediction error along one of two routes.
It may change its model to fit the world, which is perceptual inference.

Or it may change the world to fit its model, acting so as to bring about the states it predicts, which is active inference (Friston, 2010; Parr & Friston, 2018) Proximity seeking towards an attachment figure is, in these terms, a paradigm case of active inference in the following sequence.
text.formatted: Or it may change the world to fit its model, acting so as to bring about the states it predicts, which is active inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Parr & Friston, 2018)</ref> Proximity seeking towards an attachment figure is, in these terms, a paradigm case of active inference in the following sequence.

text.text: The model predicts safety or felt security as the expected, regulated state.
When a departure from the predicted state is registered as part of threat detection, meaning that the world suddenly is registered as unsafe, a prediction error is generated.

This prediction error initiates proximity seeking as the active inference response to that error, i.e., the individual acts on the world by recruiting the attachment figure to bring incoming sensory and interoceptive conditions back into line with the model's prediction of safety.
Two further constructs from this literature are required later and are introduced here.
The first is that the value of a course of action decomposes into two components.
Its pragmatic, or extrinsic, value is the expected utility of its outcomes under the agent's prior preferences.
Its epistemic value is the expected reduction in the agent's uncertainty about hidden states of the world, i.e., the information the action is expected to provide about them.
The two are weighed jointly, so an agent may select an action of low expected reward where it is predicted to yield sufficient information about hidden states (Cittern et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The two are weighed jointly, so an agent may select an action of low expected reward where it is predicted to yield sufficient information about hidden states <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Cittern et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The second construct concerns the dynamics of large-scale neuronal networks, for which two terms are often conflated (Hancock et al., 2025; Kelso, 2012).
text.formatted: The second construct concerns the dynamics of large-scale neuronal networks, for which two terms are often conflated <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Hancock et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Kelso, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: A multistable system possesses several stable attractors, i.e., several states towards which its activity tends to settle.

A metastable system moves among these attractors without being captured by any one of them for long, so that its networks integrate and segregate and several interpretations of the world remain concurrently available.

Metastability supplies a candidate neural quantity for the flexibility of inference, and its loss, in which activity is captured by a single attractor, a candidate signature of rigidity (Kotler et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Metastability supplies a candidate neural quantity for the flexibility of inference, and its loss, in which activity is captured by a single attractor, a candidate signature of rigidity <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Kotler et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Interoception, the modelling of the body's internal state, is inference: visceral signals are read against prior expectations about the body's condition and its likely trajectory (Barrett, 2017; Barrett et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Interoception, the modelling of the body's internal state, is inference: visceral signals are read against prior expectations about the body's condition and its likely trajectory <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Barrett, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Barrett et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This top-down direction is not merely interpretive but part of the regulation itself, in two respects.
First, the priors set the range of reference values against which bodily states are evaluated.
Therefore, the values the allostatic budget is directed towards are itself predicted rather than a fixed physiological given (Sterling, 2012).
text.formatted: Therefore, the values the allostatic budget is directed towards are itself predicted rather than a fixed physiological given <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Sterling, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Second, interoceptive priors condition the appraisal of exteroceptive signals, so that what counts as threatening in the world depends in part on the state the body predicts itself to be in (Barrett, 2017; Barrett et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Second, interoceptive priors condition the appraisal of exteroceptive signals, so that what counts as threatening in the world depends in part on the state the body predicts itself to be in <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Barrett, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Barrett et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Allostasis is this same inference carried through to action, which is why allostasis can be regarded as the brain's primary task (Theriault et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Allostasis is this same inference carried through to action, which is why allostasis can be regarded as the brain's primary task <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">(Theriault et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Affect and emotion are among what this inference produces.

The state of the body budget is registered in consciousness as affect, and emotions are constructed when the brain categorises these same interoceptive signals, together with the exteroceptive signals that accompany them, in the light of prior experience.
The regulation of emotion and the regulation of the body's energy budget are therefore not separable functions, and that regulation is allostasis (Barrett, 2017; Barrett et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The regulation of emotion and the regulation of the body's energy budget are therefore not separable functions, and that regulation is allostasis <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Barrett, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Barrett et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, that the object of prediction is the body does not confine the solution to it.
Because active inference resolves error by acting on the world as readily as by revising the model, an interoceptive prediction error need not be met from internal resources alone.
The interchangeability of personal and social resources that Section 2.1 imported as a premise is, on this reading, a consequence of the mechanism rather than a stipulation about it.
An internal policy and the recruitment of another are alternative routes to discharging the same interoceptive prediction error, distinguished principally by their metabolic cost.

Illness that prompts proximity seeking is the paradigm case: the error originates in the body, and the policy that discharges it is enacted in the world, through an attachment figure (Friston, 2010; Parr and Friston, 2018; Atzil et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Illness that prompts proximity seeking is the paradigm case: the error originates in the body, and the policy that discharges it is enacted in the world, through an attachment figure <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Parr and Friston, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Atzil et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Much of homeostatic, and particularly allostatic regulation is delegated to others.
Attachment is the system that manages that delegation.
Proximity seeking under distress, as the primary (secure) attachment strategy, is expedient because closeness to significant others permits coregulation.

The secondary organised strategies of attachment-system deactivation (i.e., avoidance) and hyperactivation (i.e., anxiety), and even the "tertiary disorganised strategies" of hyper-arousal and hypo-arousal, on this reading, are fallbacks when proximity seeking fails or is expected to fail.

They represent compensation strategies invoked when accessible social resources are (perceived as) unavailable or unpredictable, and are initially adaptive in that they typically hold allostatic load in check (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2008; White et al., 2023).
text.formatted: They represent compensation strategies invoked when accessible social resources are (perceived as) unavailable or unpredictable, and are initially adaptive in that they typically hold allostatic load in check <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(Mikulincer & Shaver, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">White et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, what the preceding paragraph describes, is the demand side of attachment only.
Proximity seeking is activated by threat to the self and terminates in the restoration of one's own felt security.
Its complement is the caregiving system, which Bowlby treated as an evolved behavioural system reciprocal to attachment.

It is activated whenever a significant other is perceived to be in need, and deactivated once that need is met or the recipient is judged to be protected. Canterberry and Gillath (2012) specify the dynamics of that system in a form that is directly useful here.
text.formatted: It is activated whenever a significant other is perceived to be in need, and deactivated once that need is met or the recipient is judged to be protected. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Canterberry and Gillath (2012)</ref> specify the dynamics of that system in a form that is directly useful here.

text.text: Individual differences arise at three separable points, namely in the perception of distress cues, in their interpretation, and in acting upon them.
Once distress has been registered, the sequence is organised around two decisions.
Where immediate help is available and the recipient's distress is alleviated, the system deactivates.
Where it is not, a second decision concerns whether the provision of help remains viable, and it is the answer to this question that determines which secondary strategy is adopted.

Persisting attempts to help produce caregiving hyperactivation, expressed as effortful, poorly timed and often intrusive care, whereas a judgement that further help is not feasible produces caregiving deactivation, expressed as distancing from the situation and the inhibition of empathic concern.
These strategies are measurable and are not simply the attachment strategies under a different label.

Examining the Caregiving System Scale, Colledani and colleagues (2022) found that caregiving deactivation is unidimensional whereas caregiving hyperactivation is better represented by two related but distinct constructs, namely caregiving-related worries and doubts, and intrusive or coercive caregiving.
text.formatted: Examining the Caregiving System Scale, <ref type="bibr">Colledani and colleagues (2022)</ref> found that caregiving deactivation is unidimensional whereas caregiving hyperactivation is better represented by two related but distinct constructs, namely caregiving-related worries and doubts, and intrusive or coercive caregiving.

text.text: Attachment avoidance contributed positively to deactivation and attachment anxiety to the worry and doubt component of hyperactivation only, while relationship confidence was not significantly related to either non-optimal strategy.

The correspondence between the two systems is therefore substantial but partial : an individual's caregiving regime cannot be directly and fully inferred from their attachment regime, and the two must be assessed separately.
The distinction between attachment and caregiving is consequential for a social allostatic account rather than merely taxonomic.

If co-regulation is characterised simply as bidirectional resource sharing, the interface between the attachment and caregiving systems is lost from view, and it is at that interface that the metabolic accounting is settled.

What is distributed is regulatory work, but the two partners are not performing the same work, and the costs and benefits accrue asymmetrically, ordinarily offset across repeated exchanges within an enduring relationship.
Importantly, redistributing regulatory work between two bodies does not by itself lower its total cost.
Whether co-regulation yields a net saving for the dyad, and not only for the recipient, is therefore a hypothesis of our account, and Sections 4.4 and 6 specify how it could be tested.
The cases of greatest interest here are accordingly those in which the two systems are mismatched, as when a fully activated attachment system is met by an unresponsive or depleted caregiving system.
Or when, as in the account of disruption and disorganisation, the same figure is at once the target of the attachment system and the source of the threat that activates it.

Two lines of adjacent work supply the terms in which social allostasis from an attachment perspective can be given a computational reading, and both treat the internal working models (IWMs) of attachment as priors.
The first line proposed by Cittern et al. (2018) casts IWMs as the generative models of the dyad in explicitly Bayesian terms.
text.formatted: The first line proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Cittern et al. (2018)</ref> casts IWMs as the generative models of the dyad in explicitly Bayesian terms.

text.text: They derived the organised patterns of infant attachment from the minimisation of free energy over interoceptive states, showing that an agent beginning with uninformative beliefs about caregiver responsiveness acquires organised secure, avoidant, or ambivalent (i.e., anxious) behaviour as a function of that responsiveness alone.
The same model extends to disorganisation.

Where caregiver cues are misleading, proximity seeking retains its epistemic value even when proximity is expected to increase stress, so the agent is left with an unresolved conflict between informational and regulatory demands.

The second line is the developmental construal of attachment as prediction. Tottenham and Vannucci (2025) propose that organised attachment schemas (i.e., IWMs) are abstracted from repeated pairings of the child's internal affective state, a need, with the affective outcome of the caregiver's response, so that regularities across "needs-met" pairings are internalised as secure schemas and regularities across "needs-not-met" pairings as insecure ones.
text.formatted: The second line is the developmental construal of attachment as prediction. <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">Tottenham and Vannucci (2025)</ref> propose that organised attachment schemas (i.e., IWMs) are abstracted from repeated pairings of the child's internal affective state, a need, with the affective outcome of the caregiver's response, so that regularities across "needs-met" pairings are internalised as secure schemas and regularities across "needs-not-met" pairings as insecure ones.

text.text: On their account, these pairings are initially acquired through amygdala-mediated stimulus-outcome learning and are subsequently semanticised into generalised representations carried by connections between subcortical structures and cortical midline hubs.

A complementary learning-theoretic account holds that individual differences in security are acquired through associative learning across repeated episodes of distress and caregiver response and generalised into expectations that guide later behaviour (Bosmans et al., 2020 (Bosmans et al., , 2022)).
text.formatted: A complementary learning-theoretic account holds that individual differences in security are acquired through associative learning across repeated episodes of distress and caregiver response and generalised into expectations that guide later behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Bosmans et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Bosmans et al., , 2022))</ref>.

text.text: We do not claim that it subsumes learning theory, whose account of inhibitory learning, on which new experiences of reliable support establish competing associations rather than overwriting older insecure ones, raises a question we take up below.

Both computational accounts treat the IWMs of attachment as predictions, which is the move we build upon, and both locate individual differences in the parameters of predictive models, and in particular in precision weighting.

Both are also pitched at a level, and towards an end, that differs from ours. Cittern et al. (2018) provide a computational demonstration that is agnostic about implementing circuitry. Tottenham and Vannucci (2025) provide a developmental and neuroanatomical account organised around a single cortico-subcortical axis and around the construction of attachment schemas rather than the metabolic economy those schemas serve, and they do not explicitly treat disruption, disorganisation, or trauma.
text.formatted: Both are also pitched at a level, and towards an end, that differs from ours. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Cittern et al. (2018)</ref> provide a computational demonstration that is agnostic about implementing circuitry. <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">Tottenham and Vannucci (2025)</ref> provide a developmental and neuroanatomical account organised around a single cortico-subcortical axis and around the construction of attachment schemas rather than the metabolic economy those schemas serve, and they do not explicitly treat disruption, disorganisation, or trauma.

text.text: Our account applies to attachment across the lifespan rather than in development alone, and differs in three further respects.
First, it is pitched at the level of the four NAMA modules and the two balances between them rather than at a single anatomical axis.

Second, that multinetwork architecture makes competing models expressible as a multistable system, in which an older insecure model can persist as an attractor alongside a newer secure one rather than being erased by it.
Where flexibility is preserved, activity can leave the older attractor, and the newer, context-appropriate model can govern inference.

Under stress or novelty, the basin of the older and more precisely held insecure model deepens, transitions away from it become less likely, activity is captured by it, the measured metastability of the networks should fall, and the earlier pattern re-emerges.
This is the resurfacing of insecure expectations described by inhibitory learning, given a dynamical reading, and it is what neither adjacent account is positioned to express.
Third, it makes the metabolic economy, rather than the schema, the object the computations serve.

On this basis, we propose the term social allostatic inference to denote the claim that the attachment system is one predictive-allostatic loop, that the four NAMA modules are its functional components, presented here in a heuristic order, and that organised, disrupted, and disorganised attachment are characteristic settings of the precision parameters that govern it, in association with a complementary caregiving system.
• Active inference: reducing prediction error by acting to change the world to fit the model.
• Allostasis: predictive regulation of the internal milieu, mobilising resources in anticipation of demand rather than in reaction to error.
• Allostatic load: the cumulative cost of allostatic regulation, and the point at which that cost exceeds the organism's capacity to absorb it.
• Caregiving system: the behavioural system reciprocal to attachment, activated by another's perceived need and terminating in the alleviation of that need.

• Caregiving system hyperactivation / deactivation: the two non-optimal caregiving strategies, consisting respectively of effortful and intrusive care sustained past the point at which it is warranted, and of the inhibition of concern and withdrawal from the person seeking care.
• Constructed emotion: the view that affective states are constructed by categorising interoceptive and exteroceptive signals rather than read off the body.
• Co-regulation: the regulation of one individual's physiological states through the behaviour and physiology of another.
• Free energy: a variational bound on surprise; its minimisation is the objective the system pursues.
• Hyperscanning: a method for simultaneously recording brain activity, and often other physiological and behavioural signals, from two or more participants.
It is distinct from second-person interaction, the phenomenon it is used to study.

• Incremental area under the curve (iAUC): the time-integrated deviation of a regulated signal from its baseline until a criterion return, under a standardised challenge; our operational definition of the physiological cost of a correction (Masalha et al., 2026).
text.formatted: • Incremental area under the curve (iAUC): the time-integrated deviation of a regulated signal from its baseline until a criterion return, under a standardised challenge; our operational definition of the physiological cost of a correction <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Masalha et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: • Internal working models (IWMs) of attachment: the generative model of the dyad; a prior over the availability and responsiveness of others.
statistical dependence between the neural (INS), or the behavioural, autonomic, endocrine and neural (BBS), time series of interacting individuals.
The term denotes the measured dependence and not a mechanism.
• Interoception: the sensing of the internal bodily state, construed here as itself a process of inference.

• Metastability: a dynamical regime in which no state is fully stable, so that network activity dwells transiently near former attractors without being captured by any one of them, integrates and segregates, and keeps multiple interpretations concurrently available.

• Multistability: the property of a system that possesses several stable attractors, that is, several states towards which its activity tends to settle, and between which it moves only when perturbed.
• Parental caregiving network: the distributed set of subcortical and cortical regions recruited during caregiving.
• Perceptual inference: reducing prediction error by changing the model to fit the world.
• Policy precision: the confidence with which one course of action is selected over its alternatives.
• Pragmatic and epistemic value: the value of a policy in securing preferred outcomes, and in resolving uncertainty, respectively.
• Precision: the confidence assigned to a signal or expectation, governing the weight a prediction error is granted.
We distinguish sensory (interoceptive) precision, prior precision, volatility and policy precision, each defined in this box.
• Prediction error: the mismatch between an expectation and the signal received; the currency of model correction.
• Prior: an expectation the generative model brings to bear before new evidence arrives.
Its content, for instance, whether a figure is expected to be available, is distinct from its precision.
• Prior precision: the confidence with which an expectation is held.
• Second-person interaction: real-time reciprocal engagement between individuals, in which each partner's behaviour is both a response to and a cause of the other's.
• Sensory precision: the weight granted to ascending prediction error, interoceptive when it arises from the body and exteroceptive when it arises from the world.
• Social allostasis: allostasis in which predicted demands and mobilised resources are distributed across more than one organism.

• Social allostatic inference: the proposal that attachment is one predictive-allostatic loop, with the four NAMA modules as its functional components, whose organised and disrupted patterns are settings of its precision parameters.
• Social homeostasis: conserved systems that detect and act to correct a present deficit in social connection.
• Volatility: the expected rate at which the environment changes, which sets how readily a prior is revised.
>Attachment as social allostatic inference: The single person account
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Attachment as social allostatic inference: The single person account</head>

text.text: The prototypical attachment pathway as part of NAMA is, in its most general form, a cycle of deviation from and return to a regulated state (see Figure 1) (Long et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The prototypical attachment pathway as part of NAMA is, in its most general form, a cycle of deviation from and return to a regulated state (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Long et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The reinterpretation we propose reads that cycle as active inference under a social allostatic imperative (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: The reinterpretation we propose reads that cycle as active inference under a social allostatic imperative (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: Aversion registers precision-weighted interoceptive prediction error, i.e., the surprise generated by a departure from the predicted state of felt security, whether arising from internal signals or from the bodily consequences of externally appraised threat.

Mental state representation supplies the relational priors, in the form of IWMs, that generate expectations about the availability and responsiveness of others and about one's own efficacy in recruiting them.
Approach selects the policy, most often proximity seeking, predicted to reduce that error at the lowest metabolic cost.
And emotion regulation executes the resulting allostatic correction, initially through co-regulation with an attachment figure and, with repetition, increasingly through self-regulation.

On this reading, the NAMA modules are components of one loop, and the loop's business is the predictive management of the body's energetic economy, in keeping with the proposal that allostasis is the primary charge of the brain (Theriault et al., 2025).
text.formatted: On this reading, the NAMA modules are components of one loop, and the loop's business is the predictive management of the body's energetic economy, in keeping with the proposal that allostasis is the primary charge of the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">(Theriault et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Felt security is not a signal emitted once threat has passed, but a constructed interoceptive inference, i.e., the correlate of a generative model that predicts, with high precision, that anticipated demand will be met and that the resources to meet it, whether one's own or those supplied through coregulation, are reliably available (Barrett, 2017; Barrett et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Felt security is not a signal emitted once threat has passed, but a constructed interoceptive inference, i.e., the correlate of a generative model that predicts, with high precision, that anticipated demand will be met and that the resources to meet it, whether one's own or those supplied through coregulation, are reliably available <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Barrett, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Barrett et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, felt insecurity that sustains or dismisses proximity seeking, is the correlate of a model that predicts a shortfall between demand and available regulatory resources.
Crucially, because that model is built from and continually revised against sensory and interoceptive evidence, felt security ordinarily tracks the actual state of the world.
Where the threat stems from the attachment figure, the model predicts precisely such a shortfall, which is why felt security cannot be restored while that threat persists.

External threat differs, since the presence of a reliable figure is what allows the predicted shortfall to be met, and co-regulation under external danger is the paradigm case of the attachment system functioning as intended.
We stress that this is a specification at the level of computational function and not a revision of the anatomical or neurochemical claims of our earlier work.
Simulation supports treating attachment patterns as outcomes of one inference process under different caregiving statistics.

Organised secure, avoidant, and ambivalent (i.e., anxious) behaviour emerged in a Bayesian infant as the optimal response to caregivers differing only in the probability with which they attend to a bid for proximity (Cittern et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Organised secure, avoidant, and ambivalent (i.e., anxious) behaviour emerged in a Bayesian infant as the optimal response to caregivers differing only in the probability with which they attend to a bid for proximity <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Cittern et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: That simulation varied caregiver responsiveness.
Conversely, it did not vary, and therefore could not test, where precision is attenuated within the agent, which is how we define the regimes in Section 3.3.
What we add, is the mapping of those settings onto the NAMA modules, the networks, and the neurochemistry of the loop as part of one overarching social allostatic inference mechanism.

The elements of the generative model that this mapping presupposes, namely hidden states, observations, policies, preferences and precision terms, are stated for both the attachment and the caregiving loop in Box 2, together with the direction in which each parameter moves in each regime, so that our account can be implemented and simulated.
This mapping should be read as a functional decomposition of NAMA and not as a literal process model.
Prediction, precision weighting, policy selection and regulation are recurrent and distributed, and each is expressed to some degree in every network.
What we propose, is that each computation is most heavily loaded on one NAMA module, and we present the modules in the order in which a single episode of threat and relief would engage them.
That order is heuristic.
For instance, the priors are consulted at every pass of the loop and not only after an error has been registered (Section 3.2).
The network-level part of this proposal is not new in itself.

An active inference account of second-person neuroscience has already related mutual prediction, real-time bodily adaptation and policy selection to components of the default mode, salience and frontoparietal networks and the basal ganglia (Lehmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: An active inference account of second-person neuroscience has already related mutual prediction, real-time bodily adaptation and policy selection to components of the default mode, salience and frontoparietal networks and the basal ganglia <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Lehmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: What is specific to our account, is the assignment of these computations to an ordered attachment loop, the precision regimes defined over that loop, and its caregiving complement.
This decomposition also makes claims that could be shown to be inaccurate.

It predicts that trialwise estimates of sensory precision should load on the salience network, of prior precision on the default mode network, of policy value and policy precision on cortico-basal ganglia circuitry, and of the maintenance of a selected correction on the frontoparietal network.

A pattern in which these estimates load equally on all four networks, or in which policy value and policy precision are carried by the default mode network rather than by dopaminergic midbrain and striatal circuitry (Schwartenbeck et al., 2015), would count against the decomposition and in favour of a fully distributed alternative.
text.formatted: A pattern in which these estimates load equally on all four networks, or in which policy value and policy precision are carried by the default mode network rather than by dopaminergic midbrain and striatal circuitry <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">(Schwartenbeck et al., 2015)</ref>, would count against the decomposition and in favour of a fully distributed alternative.

text.text: A second class of observation would discriminate active inference from reward-based alternatives as such.

If proximity seeking carries epistemic as well as pragmatic value, it should be sustained by uncertainty about a figure's availability and should increase as that uncertainty rises, even where its expected regulatory return is low (Cittern et al., 2018), a prediction for which the active inference literature already supplies paradigms (Lageman et al., 2026).

The architecture that the four NAMA modules describe, is assembled from domain-general large-scale networks rather than from any circuit dedicated to attachment (White et al., 2023).

text.text: The regions through which visceromotor prediction and interoceptive inference are jointly accomplished, have been delineated as a distributed allostatic-interoceptive system, mapped in cortical and subcortical detail, many of the areas among the most densely connected hubs in the brain (J. text.text: The agranular limbic cortices possess the least differentiated laminar structure and are arranged to issue, rather than receive, cortical predictions, relaying descending allostatic predictions to the hypothalamic and brainstem nuclei that regulate the autonomic, endocrine, and immune systems.
Ascending interoceptive signals, meanwhile, arrive at the granular interoceptive cortex to be compared against those predictions and yield prediction errors (Barrett, 2017; Parr & Friston, 2018).

text.text: Because this system is built from default mode and salience network regions bound by densely connected hubs, it is routinely engaged across psychological domains rather than reserved for the internal milieu, and the circuitry associated with social processing overlaps with it rather than forming a separable social system (Atzil et al., 2018; J. text.text: This is the anatomical counterpart of the claim that attachment recruits shared machinery, and it is at this system that the four NAMA modules are situated.
We take each in turn, specifying computational role, network correspondence, and the segment of the neurobiological sequence it implements, and let the synthesis table (Table 1) carry the detail.

text.text: The aversion module corresponds to the salience network (Long et al., 2020; Seeley, 2019).

text.text: Its computational role is the registration of precision-weighted prediction error, and in particular of interoceptive surprise (J. Zhang et al., 2025).

text.text: It does not detect threat as such but computes the mismatch that anticipated threat generates, and this mismatch sets the remainder of the loop in motion.

The rapid, locus coeruleus-mediated noradrenergic response that mobilises the energy and attention required to act (Izaki et al., 2024) is a candidate substrate for the precision weighting of interoceptive prediction error, since the latter requires a mechanism that adjusts the gain on prediction errors.

text.text: Its computational role is to furnish the generative model, and in particular the relational priors against which the error registered by aversion is evaluated.

The IWMs of attachment are precisely such priors, namely expectations concerning the availability and responsiveness of attachment figures and one's own efficacy in recruiting them (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2008) so that this module is where the prior precision of the loop is set.

text.text: These priors are not necessarily explicit or mentalised.
The secure base script literature holds that they are organised as temporally ordered event sequences, rather than as propositional beliefs (Waters et al., 1998; Waters & Waters, 2006).

text.text: Because these priors are consulted at every pass of the loop rather than at a single moment, this module is less tightly bound to one segment of the neurobiological sequence than the others.

Its clearest neurochemical footprint is the proposed catecholaminergic and oxytocinergic retrieval of the attachment figure's identity from episodic memory, a mechanism that remains to be established empirically (Izaki et al., 2024).

text.text: The approach module corresponds to the cortico-basal ganglia reward circuit (Haber & Knutson, 2010; Long et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The approach module corresponds to the cortico-basal ganglia reward circuit <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Haber & Knutson, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Long et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Its computational role is policy selection, and it is the locus at which active inference is selected and initiated.

Confronted with an error registered by aversion and evaluated against the priors supplied by mental state representation, the system may reduce that error by acting to change the world, and the paradigmatic policy it selects, is proximity seeking towards an attachment figure, i.e., the action predicted to return the body to its regulated state at the lowest anticipated cost.

Policy value here is not exhausted by that pragmatic component: proximity seeking also carries epistemic value, since approaching the figure resolves uncertainty about their availability and responsiveness.

Their divergence is what we take up in the case of disruption and disorganisation, where misleading cues can preserve the epistemic value of approach even as its pragmatic value turns negative (Cittern et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Their divergence is what we take up in the case of disruption and disorganisation, where misleading cues can preserve the epistemic value of approach even as its pragmatic value turns negative <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Cittern et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The dopaminergic signalling that supplies the decision and the motivation to move, redirected from undirected flight to "social flight" towards a specific figure, is in incentive terms the "wanting" that drives policy selection and its maintenance through sustained D1-mediated signalling in ventral striatal and nigral circuits, which subsides only when reward is obtained at reunion (Izaki et al., 2024).

text.text: Finally, the emotion regulation module corresponds to the frontoparietal, or central executive, network (Long et al., 2020; Seeley et al., 2007).

text.text: Its computational role is the execution of the allostatic correction, the high-level control operation through which the predicted return to the regulated state is brought about and stabilised and through which the precision of competing signals is adjusted so that the selected policy can be carried through.
This is plausibly the most metabolically expensive operation in the loop, since sustained topdown control is particularly costly (Theriault et al., 2025).

text.text: The distinction between coregulation and self-regulation is a distinction in where the correction is performed, not in its computational character.

In early development, and in the prototypical case throughout life, much of the correction is supplied by the attachment figure, whose regulatory action furnishes the conditions the individual's model predicts will restore the regulated state, at what Social Baseline Theory proposes, is a lower cost than solitary regulation would exact (Beckes and Coan, 2011; Coan and Sbarra, 2015; Saxbe et al., 2020).

text.text: The developmental transition from coregulation to self-regulation is, in these terms, a gradual transfer of regulatory labour, as the priors and control operations initially exercised by the caregiver are internalised and the individual becomes able to perform alone the correction formerly performed jointly.

text.text: NAMA does not treat the modules as independent but organises them around two reciprocal balances: between the affective evaluation and the cognitive control systems, and, within affective evaluation, between the aversion and approach modules (Long et al., 2020).

text.text: Redescribed as one loop, these balances become a message passing within a predictive hierarchy, in which lower levels convey ascending prediction errors and higher levels return descending predictions, with the exchange weighted at each stage by precision (Friston, 2010; Parr and Friston, 2018).
text.formatted: Redescribed as one loop, these balances become a message passing within a predictive hierarchy, in which lower levels convey ascending prediction errors and higher levels return descending predictions, with the exchange weighted at each stage by precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Parr and Friston, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The balance between affective evaluation and cognitive control is then the balance between the weight granted to the ascending error registered by aversion and the weight granted to the descending priors supplied by mental state representation and the control exercised by emotion regulation.

And the balance between aversion and approach is the balance within the error-driven system between registering a prediction error and committing to a policy that would discharge it, that is, between perceptual and active inference (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: And the balance between aversion and approach is the balance within the error-driven system between registering a prediction error and committing to a policy that would discharge it, that is, between perceptual and active inference (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: Neither balance is a fixed anatomical property.
Each is set dynamically by the precision assigned to the signals passing between modules.

A prior is a distribution rather than a point estimate, so a securely calibrated prior encodes availability as highly probable rather than certain, and an isolated non-response generates an error small enough to be absorbed without revision.

That revision only follows when accumulated prediction error exceeds what the precision of the prior can absorb, which depends jointly on the magnitude of the departures and the confidence with which the prior is held, and on the volatility the system expects, since an agent that expects its environment to change, grants recent evidence more weight and revises its priors more readily (Mathys et al., 2011).
text.formatted: That revision only follows when accumulated prediction error exceeds what the precision of the prior can absorb, which depends jointly on the magnitude of the departures and the confidence with which the prior is held, and on the volatility the system expects, since an agent that expects its environment to change, grants recent evidence more weight and revises its priors more readily <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Mathys et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This is what allows attachment representations to be stable under ordinary variation yet revisable under sustained change.
Secure attachment corresponds to calibrated precision.
The priors supplied by mental state representation encode the attachment figure as reliably available and are held with a precision that matches that reliability.

In doing so, they neither resist correction inappropriately nor collapse under transient evidence, while interoceptive prediction errors are weighted such that genuine departures recruit the loop, but momentary fluctuations do not.

Because the priors are accurate, the initiating error is resolved efficiently, frequently through co-regulation, and the loop terminates promptly once the high-precision prediction of met demand that constitutes felt security is reinstated.
On our account, this is the regime that minimises the long-run metabolic cost of regulation, a hypothesis whose test we specify in Section 6.

The premise of this hypothesis, though not the hypothesis itself, has recent support: the presence of a close partner lowered the physiological cost of standard homeostatic challenges on average, while a subset of participants regulated less efficiently in the partner's presence (Masalha et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The premise of this hypothesis, though not the hypothesis itself, has recent support: the presence of a close partner lowered the physiological cost of standard homeostatic challenges on average, while a subset of participants regulated less efficiently in the partner's presence <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Masalha et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, this work did not assess attachment, and our account predicts that such individual differences vary with the attachment and caregiving regimes of the two partners.
Anxious, or hyperactivating, attachment corresponds to a regime in which aversion prediction error is chronically over-weighted while the prior concerning availability is held with low precision.
Intermittent caregiving installs not a confident expectation of unavailability but a diffuse one: the figure is expected to respond with a probability that is neither high nor reliably estimable.
Because intermittent caregiving is also changeable caregiving, the same history installs a high estimate of volatility.
Policy precision is correspondingly low, so approach and protest alternate rather than resolve, which is the computational form of ambivalence.
A diffuse prior under high volatility updates readily, which means that reassurance can shift it.

What it does not do, is consolidate, since an agent that expects its environment to change, discounts earlier evidence as soon as the next ambiguous cue arrives, and the prior returns towards its diffuse state.
The loop is therefore terminated by reassurance only briefly, and not durably, as in the secure regime.
Proximity seeking is thus sustained beyond the point at which it has already procured co-regulation.

The affiliative appearance of hyperactivation should not, however, be mistaken for the low-cost sociality of the secure regime, since its cost is borne as chronic over-recruitment of the loop and, over time, as the accumulation of social allostatic load (Saxbe et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The affiliative appearance of hyperactivation should not, however, be mistaken for the low-cost sociality of the secure regime, since its cost is borne as chronic over-recruitment of the loop and, over time, as the accumulation of social allostatic load <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">(Saxbe et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Box 2 states the parameter settings of this and the other regimes, and the observations that would distinguish them.
The volatility prediction can fail.

In a dynamic trust game, individuals with elevated anxiety learned less from negative social outcomes and did not raise their learning rate as uncertainty rose (Lamba et al., 2020), which is the opposite of the pattern we assign to the anxious regime.
text.formatted: In a dynamic trust game, individuals with elevated anxiety learned less from negative social outcomes and did not raise their learning rate as uncertainty rose <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Lamba et al., 2020)</ref>, which is the opposite of the pattern we assign to the anxious regime.

text.text: Anxiety in that study was not attachment anxiety, and whether attachment anxiety behaves likewise is therefore the first falsifier in Box 2 that should be tested.
Avoidant, or deactivating, attachment corresponds to the converse regime, in which social prediction error is down-weighed, and regulation is displaced onto costly individual correction.

The priors encode attachment figures as unavailable, or the recruitment of others as ineffective, so that proximity seeking is assigned a low expected value and the precision granted to social prediction error is attenuated at source.

Unlike the anxious regime, this prior is held with high precision: consistently unavailable caregiving supports a confident negative expectation, whereas inconsistently available caregiving supports only a diffuse one.
The two insecure strategies therefore attenuate precision at different points in the hierarchy, avoidance at the level of ascending error and anxiety at the level of the descending prior.
The composure that the avoidant regime presents, is therefore a relocation of regulatory work and not its absence.
The relocation is visible physiologically from infancy.

In the Strange Situation, infants classified as avoidant showed greater vagal withdrawal and higher salivary alpha-amylase than secure infants, despite their behavioural composure (Hill-Soderlund et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In the Strange Situation, infants classified as avoidant showed greater vagal withdrawal and higher salivary alpha-amylase than secure infants, despite their behavioural composure <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Hill-Soderlund et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: It nonetheless forgoes the metabolic economy of the social baseline and is, on that reasoning, more expensive to sustain over time even where it presents as composed (Coan and Sbarra, 2015).

text.text: The nearest existing test is longitudinal.

Infants classified as insecure in the Strange Situation Procedure, whether anxious-resistant or anxious-avoidant, were more likely than those classified as secure to report an inflammation-related illness three decades later (Puig et al., 2013), and adult attachment orientations have been associated with inflammatory and cellular immune markers (Ehrlich, 2019).

text.text: Meta-analytically, early insecurity has been associated with heightened RSA and cortisol reactivity upon reunion (Groh & Narayan, 2019).
text.formatted: Meta-analytically, early insecurity has been associated with heightened RSA and cortisol reactivity upon reunion <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Groh & Narayan, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are consistent with a greater long-run cost of insecurity but do not isolate avoidance, since the longitudinal association held for both insecure classifications.
The prediction specific to the avoidant regime, that self-reliant regulation is costlier than delegated regulation at a matched regulatory outcome, therefore remains untested.
The second prediction in Box 2, a lower learning rate for social than for nonsocial outcomes, is also not yet supported.

In a differential fear-conditioning paradigm, the safety value of the attachment figure was reduced in more avoidant individuals, whereas the rate of new safety learning was not (Camerman et al., 2023), which locates the avoidant difference in the content of the prior rather than in the rate at which new evidence is learned.
