text.text: B. Parameter settings of each regime (hypotheses) Each entry states the direction of the four precision terms and the content of the prior, the prediction that follows, and the observation that would count against it.

• Secure: sensory precision calibrated to the informativeness of the signal; attachment figures expected to be available, with prior precision matched to the figures' reliability; an accurate volatility estimate; high policy precision for the social policy when demand is present.
Prediction: prompt termination, a lower cost of a matched correction with the figure present, and synchrony that rises with demand and is released.
Would count against it: no cost difference between secure and insecure dyads at a matched regulatory outcome.

• Anxious (hyperactivating): high sensory precision on threat-related error; attachment figures' availability uncertain; low prior precision; a high volatility estimate; low policy precision, so that approach and protest alternate.

Prediction: in probabilistic learning with attachment-relevant feedback, a higher volatility estimate (Mathys et al., 2011) and updating that is fast but does not consolidate; a high mean and high within-dyad variability of synchrony.
text.formatted: Prediction: in probabilistic learning with attachment-relevant feedback, a higher volatility estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Mathys et al., 2011)</ref> and updating that is fast but does not consolidate; a high mean and high within-dyad variability of synchrony.

text.text: Would count against it: volatility estimates not elevated relative to secure individuals, or slow updating.

• Avoidant (deactivating): low sensory precision on social prediction error; attachment figures unavailable, or recruitment ineffective; high prior precision; a low volatility estimate; high policy precision for the individual policy and low for the social policy.
Prediction: a lower learning rate for social than for matched nonsocial outcomes, synchrony low and unresponsive to demand, and a higher cost of self-regulation at a matched outcome.
Would count against it: equal social and nonsocial learning rates, or self-regulation not costlier than delegated regulation at a matched outcome.

• Maltreatment route: high sensory precision; a multimodal prior in which the same figures are represented as safe haven and as threat, with high precision on each mode; volatility not specified; each policy well specified, with arbitration between them failing.
Prediction: contradiction where two modes compete, and disorientation where more than two do, with synchrony entered and abandoned within an episode.
Would count against it: no relation between the behavioural profile and the heterogeneity of caregiving configurations.
• Neglect route: low (blunted) sensory precision; a prior of the futility of action held with high precision; a low volatility estimate; low policy precision across social and solitary policies.
Prediction: reduced sensitivity to controllability in nonsocial as well as social tasks, and hypo-arousal.
Would count against it: intact detection of controllability in nonsocial tasks (Maier & Seligman, 2016).
text.formatted: Would count against it: intact detection of controllability in nonsocial tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Maier & Seligman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The two disruption routes are the most speculative entries, and their links to hyper-arousal and hypo-arousal are hypotheses whose direction may depend on developmental timing (Section 3.4).
The organised styles are regulatory shifts within an otherwise functioning assignment of precision.

Attachment disruption and disorganisation is better described as a departure from that assignment (White et al., 2020), and the NAMDA distinction between the consequences of maltreatment versus those of neglect corresponds to two different failures of the loop.
text.formatted: Attachment disruption and disorganisation is better described as a departure from that assignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">(White et al., 2020)</ref>, and the NAMDA distinction between the consequences of maltreatment versus those of neglect corresponds to two different failures of the loop.

text.text: The two routes are dissociable at their origin but not mutually exclusive in their course, and they do not constitute a diagnostic mapping, particularly because the disorganised classification has low specificity and low sensitivity with respect to maltreatment (Granqvist et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The two routes are dissociable at their origin but not mutually exclusive in their course, and they do not constitute a diagnostic mapping, particularly because the disorganised classification has low specificity and low sensitivity with respect to maltreatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Granqvist et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore describe the two routes as mechanisms of loop failure rather than as inferences from behaviour to cause.

Each step in what follows, from a caregiving history to a computational regime, from that regime to hyperarousal or hypoarousal, and from these to dissociation, is a hypothesis, and the low specificity of disorganisation for maltreatment applies to every one of them.

Nonetheless, what the two routes share, is that the IWMs issue their predictions largely in advance of, and irrespective of, the current interaction, whereas in the organised styles, they remain priors that incoming evidence can in principle correct.

Where the attachment figure is at once the source of threat and the figure to whom proximity would ordinarily be sought, which is the configuration that maltreatment installs, the model that accumulates is neither unimodal nor diffuse but multimodal.

The same figure is represented under several mutually incompatible predictions, i.e., as safe haven, as threat, as unresponsive, as itself frightened, each held with high precision because each has been repeatedly confirmed by a recurring configuration of care.
The corresponding policies are therefore each well specified and jointly unexecutable.
The behavioural signature follows from the number of modes as well as their precision.

Where two policies of comparable precision compete, the output is contradiction or its limiting case, arrest, i.e., approach initiated and reversed, contact sought while orientation is averted, action interrupted mid-sequence, or freezing where neither policy prevails.

Where more than two compete, arbitration does not merely reverse but fails to stabilise, and fragments of several policies surface in succession, which is what presents as disorientation, contextually anomalous action, and stereotypy (Duschinsky & Solomon, 2017; Granqvist et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Where more than two compete, arbitration does not merely reverse but fails to stabilise, and fragments of several policies surface in succession, which is what presents as disorientation, contextually anomalous action, and stereotypy <ref type="bibr">(Duschinsky & Solomon, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Granqvist et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The number of modes is not a free parameter but reflects the number of distinct caregiving configurations consolidated with sufficient frequency to acquire precision in their own right, which yields the prediction that more heterogeneous caregiving should shift the profile from contradiction toward disorientation.
It is worth marking the level at which these claims are pitched.

Disorganisation is described at three levels that are not always distinguished, namely the Strange Situation Procedure classification, the system-level failure to sustain a coherent strategy under alarm, and the observable behaviours that may occur below classification threshold (Duschinsky & Solomon, 2017; Frau, 2026).
text.formatted: Disorganisation is described at three levels that are not always distinguished, namely the Strange Situation Procedure classification, the system-level failure to sustain a coherent strategy under alarm, and the observable behaviours that may occur below classification threshold <ref type="bibr">(Duschinsky & Solomon, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Frau, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: What we have described, concerns the second and the third, and bears on the first only inasmuch as the classification is assigned based on the behaviours.

A brainstem-based account derives the same behavioural signature from competition among incompatible sensorimotor action programmes, none of which achieves stable dominance, so that contradictory movement, interrupted sequences and freezing follow from a failure of arbitration rather than from a deficit of representation or of top-down regulation (Frau, 2026).
text.formatted: A brainstem-based account derives the same behavioural signature from competition among incompatible sensorimotor action programmes, none of which achieves stable dominance, so that contradictory movement, interrupted sequences and freezing follow from a failure of arbitration rather than from a deficit of representation or of top-down regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Frau, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: That account locates the motor expression of the competition in midbrain circuitry, principally the superior colliculus in interaction with the periaqueductal grey.
We take the two accounts to be complementary, ours specifying that arbitration fails and theirs where the resulting conflict is realised in action.

A complementary formalisation locates the failure in the epistemic rather than the pragmatic term, in that disrupted affective communication sustains a high epistemic value for a proximity seeking whose ambiguity approach continues to promise to resolve (Cittern et al., 2018), which is also what prevents the competing modes from being extinguished, since each retains the informational value that would come from resolving it.
text.formatted: A complementary formalisation locates the failure in the epistemic rather than the pragmatic term, in that disrupted affective communication sustains a high epistemic value for a proximity seeking whose ambiguity approach continues to promise to resolve <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Cittern et al., 2018)</ref>, which is also what prevents the competing modes from being extinguished, since each retains the informational value that would come from resolving it.

text.text: What consolidates across repetition is narrower: of the competing modes, only the prediction of threat is never disconfirmed, and it is that mode which comes to dominate.

Moreover, because the error is never discharged, the sensory data of these episodes are assigned a high precision that subsequent evidence is not granted the weight to revise, and the IWM that accumulates comes to predict threat as imminent by default.
This is the state we hypothesise to underlie hyperarousal in NAMDA, arising specifically from the maltreatment route (White et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This is the state we hypothesise to underlie hyperarousal in NAMDA, arising specifically from the maltreatment route <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">(White et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Flexibility is, accordingly, compromised twice on this route, within episodes because activity switches among competing attractors without settling on any, and across development because it is captured by a single one.
Finally, our use of hyperarousal is attachment specific.

In the computational trauma literature, hyperarousal is formalised as an excessive readiness of defensive policy following from prior aversions held with unduly high precision, and the prior is shielded because defensive action removes the organism from the situation that could disconfirm it (Kotler et al., 2026; Linson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In the computational trauma literature, hyperarousal is formalised as an excessive readiness of defensive policy following from prior aversions held with unduly high precision, and the prior is shielded because defensive action removes the organism from the situation that could disconfirm it <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Kotler et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Linson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the attachment-specific case, the competing policies prevent any action from being completed, so that no disconfirming evidence is generated at all.
The neglect route differs in kind.

Where care is reliably absent rather than itself threatening, no approach-avoidance conflict arises, and the initiating prediction error instead fails to be discharged because proximity seeking does not procure the co-regulation it predicts.
The IWMs that accumulate encode not danger in the figure but the futility of action, the expectation that no available policy will resolve the deviation.
Where that expectation generalises across the policy space, the loop ceases to invest in regulation altogether.

In the terms of Section 2.2, the expectation of futility is itself held with high prior precision, since reliably absent care confirms it without exception, and what falls is policy precision, across social and solitary policies alike, so that no course of action is selected with confidence, and the system disengages.
Crucially, this should not be mistaken for the avoidant regime.
Avoidance also discounts the value of turning to others, but it takes the regulatory work back onto itself and continues to perform it, at considerable cost.
Here, that work is not relocated but relinquished.
Avoidant caregiving still offers a partner from whom the operations of regulation can be internalised, and avoidance learns that others will not help, which leaves solitary action intact.
Neglect learns something about action itself, namely that it does not alter outcomes, and this has no reason to stop at the boundary between social and solitary policies.
The system therefore withdraws from self-regulation as well, which is the difference between an expensive strategy and no strategy at all.

As such, the resulting presentation of neglect, i.e., low in energy, blunted, and often dissociative, is better described as a metabolic conservation in the face of a body budget already in deficit than as a dedicated immobilisation mechanism, which is consistent with the finding that the passivity produced by uncontrollable aversive events is a default response that the detection of control would otherwise inhibit (Maier & Seligman, 2016).
text.formatted: As such, the resulting presentation of neglect, i.e., low in energy, blunted, and often dissociative, is better described as a metabolic conservation in the face of a body budget already in deficit than as a dedicated immobilisation mechanism, which is consistent with the finding that the passivity produced by uncontrollable aversive events is a default response that the detection of control would otherwise inhibit <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Maier & Seligman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This is the state we hypothesise to underlie hypoarousal in NAMDA (White et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This is the state we hypothesise to underlie hypoarousal in NAMDA <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">(White et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the two routes of maltreatment and neglect are dissociable at their origin but are not mutually exclusive in their course.

Hypoarousal can follow hyperarousal where activation is sustained beyond what the energetic budget can support, in which case the collapse of policy precision is the terminal phase of a regime that began as its opposite.

We hypothesise that the transition has neuroendocrine content, since chronic threat exposure is associated with suppression and habituation of HPA-axis output (Miller et al., 2007) and with downregulated dopaminergic function, which is not a return to regulation but a costly failure state, and the source of the anergia and blunted motivation the presentation displays.
text.formatted: We hypothesise that the transition has neuroendocrine content, since chronic threat exposure is associated with suppression and habituation of HPA-axis output <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Miller et al., 2007)</ref> and with downregulated dopaminergic function, which is not a return to regulation but a costly failure state, and the source of the anergia and blunted motivation the presentation displays.

text.text: The same sequence may apply to the neglect route itself.
Blunted diurnal cortisol has been reported in preschool children with a history of child protective services involvement (Bernard, Zwerling, et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Blunted diurnal cortisol has been reported in preschool children with a history of child protective services involvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bernard, Zwerling, et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: At 4 months, by contrast, maternal childhood neglect, but not abuse, has been associated with higher infant cortisol output during the Still-Face Paradigm (Khoury et al., 2026).
text.formatted: At 4 months, by contrast, maternal childhood neglect, but not abuse, has been associated with higher infant cortisol output during the Still-Face Paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Khoury et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Maternal neglect history combined with disoriented caregiving predicted higher infant cortisol output, and maternal abuse history combined with negative-intrusive caregiving predicted lower output (Chasson et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Maternal neglect history combined with disoriented caregiving predicted higher infant cortisol output, and maternal abuse history combined with negative-intrusive caregiving predicted lower output <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Chasson et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These designs index the mother's history and current caregiving rather than the infant's own maltreatment.

Even so, at the level of infant cortisol, they run opposite to the arousal profiles we have assigned to the two routes, and they accord with the proposal that, in infancy, the absence of the caregiver is itself the primary threat (Lyons-Ruth et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Even so, at the level of infant cortisol, they run opposite to the arousal profiles we have assigned to the two routes, and they accord with the proposal that, in infancy, the absence of the caregiver is itself the primary threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Lyons-Ruth et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The mapping of the two routes onto hyper-and hypoarousal should therefore be treated as agedependent, with hypoarousal on the neglect route a later phase rather than its starting point.
We tentatively place dissociation here as well.

Its association with severity of childhood abuse, mediated in part by disorganised attachment (Byun et al., 2016), fits the terminal phase of the maltreatment route rather than neglect proper, and we therefore predict dissociative presentations to concentrate where hypoarousal follows a sustained hyperaroused regime rather than where care was simply absent.
text.formatted: Its association with severity of childhood abuse, mediated in part by disorganised attachment <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Byun et al., 2016)</ref>, fits the terminal phase of the maltreatment route rather than neglect proper, and we therefore predict dissociative presentations to concentrate where hypoarousal follows a sustained hyperaroused regime rather than where care was simply absent.

text.text: 3.5 The caregiving system as a second instance of the loop: a testable extension of NAMA Sections 3.1 to 3.4 describe the attachment system, and the account would be incomplete if the complementary system named in Section 2.4 were carried into the dyadic argument without a corresponding specification.
Caregiving is a single-brain system in the same sense that attachment is, and we therefore treat it here (see Figure 2 and Table 2).
text.formatted: Caregiving is a single-brain system in the same sense that attachment is, and we therefore treat it here (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref> and Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: We propose, as a testable extension of NAMA, that caregiving is a second instance of the same loop rather than a separate architecture.
The anatomical evidence is consistent with this proposal.

Reviewing the neural mechanisms of paternal care across species, Feldman and colleagues (2019) describe the subcortical structures that support maternal caregiving as having been elaborated into a global network of parental care, and characterise paternal behaviour as highly malleable, accompanied by substantial neural plasticity, and shaped by prior and current caregiving experience as well as by infant and ecological input.
text.formatted: Reviewing the neural mechanisms of paternal care across species, <ref type="bibr">Feldman and colleagues (2019)</ref> describe the subcortical structures that support maternal caregiving as having been elaborated into a global network of parental care, and characterise paternal behaviour as highly malleable, accompanied by substantial neural plasticity, and shaped by prior and current caregiving experience as well as by infant and ecological input.

text.text: Human parental brain findings partition that network in a manner that maps onto our modules.

Comparing primary caregiving mothers, secondary caregiving fathers and primary caregiving fathers, Abraham and colleagues (2014) reported that parenting integrated the functioning of a set of subcortical and paralimbic structures implicated in emotional processing, and cortical structures implicated in social understanding, with amygdala and superior temporal sulcus activation weighted differently across the groups and their functional connectivity scaling with time spent in direct childcare.  1 and Box 2 carry the detail.
text.formatted: Comparing primary caregiving mothers, secondary caregiving fathers and primary caregiving fathers, <ref type="bibr">Abraham and colleagues (2014)</ref> reported that parenting integrated the functioning of a set of subcortical and paralimbic structures implicated in emotional processing, and cortical structures implicated in social understanding, with amygdala and superior temporal sulcus activation weighted differently across the groups and their functional connectivity scaling with time spent in direct childcare.  <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> and Box 2 carry the detail.

text.text: Panel (B) is a two-dimensional projection onto sensory (interoceptive) precision and prior precision.

Volatility, policy precision and the content of the prior are not represented on its axes, and the neglect route, which is defined by low policy precision under a highprecision prior of futility, is placed by annotation.
That the organised styles are recoverable as parameter settings of a single loop has been shown in simulation (Cittern et al., 2018).
text.formatted: That the organised styles are recoverable as parameter settings of a single loop has been shown in simulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Cittern et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Read through the loop, the four NAMA modules take the following caregiving side roles, and we state them as a proposal to be tested rather than as an established mapping.

Aversion registers the other's signalled distress as a precision-weighted prediction error, i.e., as a mismatch between the recipient's inferred state and the state the caregiver's model predicts for them.
Mental state representation supplies the caregiving side priors, comprising expectations about the recipient's needs, about the efficacy of one's own care, and about one's standing as a caregiver.

Approach selects the caregiving policy, and emotion regulation executes the correction, which on this side includes the regulation of the caregiver's own distress at the recipient's distress, since the correction cannot be delivered by a caregiver whose own loop has been recruited by it.

Reviews of the human parental brain independently distinguish reward and motivation systems, salience and threat systems, regulatory systems, and systems for empathy and mentalizing (Swain et al., 2014), which is the same fourfold division arrived at from a different starting point.
text.formatted: Reviews of the human parental brain independently distinguish reward and motivation systems, salience and threat systems, regulatory systems, and systems for empathy and mentalizing <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">(Swain et al., 2014)</ref>, which is the same fourfold division arrived at from a different starting point.

text.text: What our account adds, is the organisation of that partition as one loop, and the claim that the settings governing the transitions between its stages are what individual differences consist of.
One asymmetry between the two instances is computational rather than anatomical and, in our view, carries the most weight.
Both loops proceed by inference.
On the account given in Section 2.3, the bodily state the attachment loop regulates, is itself inferred rather than read off.
The difference lies in the evidence each has to work with.

The attachment loop is served by interoceptive afferents arising in the same body whose state it regulates, whereas the caregiving loop must infer a state in another body from exteroceptive evidence, e.g., cry, face, posture, voice, and later speech.

The caregiver accumulates a model of this particular recipient across repeated episodes, and the accuracy of that model is itself learned, and therefore varies across caregivers and improves with experience to a degree that the accuracy of inference about one's own body need not.

The caregiving loop's precision on its initiating error is thus a function of dyad-specific learning, which is why mental state representation occupies a more load-bearing position on the caregiving side than on the attachment side, and why the same signal may be read correctly by one caregiver and not by another.
The two instances are not sealed off from one another within a single brain.

For example, maternal attachment representations have been shown to predict caregiving side neural responses to one's own infant, with securely attached mothers showing stronger activation of the ventral striatum and the oxytocin-associated hypothalamic and pituitary region to their own infant's faces than mothers classified as insecure-dismissing on the Adult Attachment Interview (Strathearn et al., 2009).
text.formatted: For example, maternal attachment representations have been shown to predict caregiving side neural responses to one's own infant, with securely attached mothers showing stronger activation of the ventral striatum and the oxytocin-associated hypothalamic and pituitary region to their own infant's faces than mothers classified as insecure-dismissing on the Adult Attachment Interview <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">(Strathearn et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern is consistent with our account, since the priors an individual holds about the availability and efficacy of others are not obviously partitioned by which loop consults them.
We note it here as a point requiring development, because it implies that the parameters of the two instances are linked in ways the present formulation does not yet specify.
The two non-optimal caregiving strategies can then be read as precision regimes in the same terms as the organised attachment styles of Section 3.3.

Caregiving deactivation attenuates, at source, the precision granted to the recipient's signals, so that a demand does not register as warranting investment, and the withheld investment is intelligible as a policy predicted to fail.
Caregiving hyperactivation over-weights those signals or holds a prior that assigns high probability to unmet need, so that investment is made out of proportion to demand.
Neural evidence bears on the latter directly.

Comparing synchronous and intrusive mothers, Atzil and colleagues (2011) found that synchronous caregiving was characterised by nucleus accumbens activation functionally connected with social-cognitive and empathy networks and by temporally organised activity, whereas intrusive caregiving was characterised by amygdala activation functionally connected with action-oriented regions and by less organised temporal patterns.
text.formatted: Comparing synchronous and intrusive mothers, <ref type="bibr">Atzil and colleagues (2011)</ref> found that synchronous caregiving was characterised by nucleus accumbens activation functionally connected with social-cognitive and empathy networks and by temporally organised activity, whereas intrusive caregiving was characterised by amygdala activation functionally connected with action-oriented regions and by less organised temporal patterns.

text.text: Read through the loop, intrusive care is not simply care in excess, but aversion over-weighted and approach engaged without integration with mental state representation, i.e., a failure of the balance between affective evaluation and cognitive control rather than a setting on any one module.

The two-component structure that Colledani et al. (2022) recover, is informative here, since caregiving-related worry and doubt is naturally read as low precision on the prior concerning one's own efficacy, whereas intrusive and coercive care is naturally read as a policy sustained past the evidence that it is required.
text.formatted: The two-component structure that <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Colledani et al. (2022)</ref> recover, is informative here, since caregiving-related worry and doubt is naturally read as low precision on the prior concerning one's own efficacy, whereas intrusive and coercive care is naturally read as a policy sustained past the evidence that it is required.

text.text: On this reading, the two components are not two indicators of one construct, but two distinct parameter settings, which would explain why only the former was associated with attachment anxiety.

That these settings are modifiable, is indicated by randomised intervention trials, in which attachment-based programmes targeting caregiver behaviour were followed by more normative cortisol regulation in the child than a control intervention (Berlin et al., 2019; Bernard, Dozier, et al., 2015).
text.formatted: That these settings are modifiable, is indicated by randomised intervention trials, in which attachment-based programmes targeting caregiver behaviour were followed by more normative cortisol regulation in the child than a control intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Berlin et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bernard, Dozier, et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In one trial, the difference in cortisol regulation in middle childhood was statistically mediated by observed parental sensitivity (Garnett et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In one trial, the difference in cortisol regulation in middle childhood was statistically mediated by observed parental sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Garnett et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Reading the change in sensitivity as a recalibration of caregiving-side precision is our interpretation and was not measured.

What the trials show, is that a change in caregiver behaviour is followed by an allostatic change in the other body, which is consistent with the two loops being linked through regulation and not only through behaviour.
Two limits should be stated.

First, the human parental brain literature is predominantly maternal and the paternal literature smaller and more recent (Abraham & Feldman, 2022), and the caregiving strategy measures show partial rather than full invariance across gender (Colledani et al., 2022; Feldman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: First, the human parental brain literature is predominantly maternal and the paternal literature smaller and more recent <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abraham & Feldman, 2022)</ref>, and the caregiving strategy measures show partial rather than full invariance across gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Colledani et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Feldman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The mapping proposed here should therefore not be assumed to hold uniformly across caregivers.
Second, no study we are aware of has assessed the four NAMA modules jointly on the caregiving side, so the partition rests on convergence between separate literatures rather than on a single design.
The convergence is notable, although the evidence remains predominantly correlational, and the organisation we propose has not been tested directly.
We therefore treat the caregiving loop throughout as a testable extension of NAMA and not as an established architecture.

Every step of the argument to this point has been pitched at the level of one brain, and the loop has been closed inside one head, even where the regulatory work it describes is supplied through caregiving by somebody else.

Because attachment is for co-regulation, and the unit in which co-regulation occurs is the dyad, an attachment account confined to one brain describes only half of the process (Long et al., 2020; Redcay & Schilbach, 2019; Schilbach et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Because attachment is for co-regulation, and the unit in which co-regulation occurs is the dyad, an attachment account confined to one brain describes only half of the process <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Long et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Redcay & Schilbach, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Schilbach et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: That limitation takes a second and more specific form.
The loop specified in Section 3 describes the attachment system alone.

The partner in an interacting dyad is ordinarily not running a second copy of that loop, but the complementary caregiving system, which is activated by another's signalled or anticipated distress or vulnerability and terminates in the alleviation of that distress (Sections 2.4 and 3.5).
Moving the account to the dyad therefore requires two extensions i.e., from a single brain to two, and from a single system to its complement (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: Moving the account to the dyad therefore requires two extensions i.e., from a single brain to two, and from a single system to its complement (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>).

text.text: The evidence we draw upon, comes from the hyperscanning and synchrony literatures, whose central quantities we define at the outset of Section 4.2.

What those measures can and cannot capture, has been examined at length elsewhere (Burgess, 2013; Chidichimo et al., 2026; De Felice et al., 2025; Hakim et al., 2023; Hamilton, 2021; Holroyd, 2022; Novembre & Iannetti, 2021).

text.text: Accordingly, the mismatches between the attachment and caregiving systems identified in Section 2.4, and projected onto the dyad in Section 4.5, are a specific case of misattunement, one in which the two partners run different systems with different activating and terminating conditions.
We keep two things apart throughout.
Hyperscanning is a method for recording two or more individuals' brain activity simultaneously, and second-person interaction is the behavioural phenomenon of interest.

Simultaneous recording does not by itself establish that an interaction was reciprocal, and synchrony between two recordings does not by itself establish that the partners were interacting at all (Section 4.2).
Two existing accounts formalise the relations at issue, and we adopt an element of each.
The first is an active inference treatment of dyadic interaction (Lehmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The first is an active inference treatment of dyadic interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Lehmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Where two brains interact in real time, each infers the causes of the sensations the other generates, and the partners align their generative models through the reciprocal exchange of predictions and prediction errors.

Attunement of the interoceptive and proprioceptive systems is driven by the demands of the exchange rather than accompanying it incidentally, which places bodily regulation inside the alignment rather than alongside it.
Prediction error within the dyad falls by two routes, which correspond to the perceptual and active branches of inference distinguished in Section 2.2.

A partner may revise their model to fit the other, which is the acquisition of partner-specific accuracy across repeated encounters, or may instead act such that their own conduct conforms more closely to what the other predicts.

Both features bear on our argument, since the encoding and resolution of prediction error is metabolically costly (Theriault et al., 2025), and alignment of this kind is therefore bioenergetic and not only informational.
text.formatted: Both features bear on our argument, since the encoding and resolution of prediction error is metabolically costly <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">(Theriault et al., 2025)</ref>, and alignment of this kind is therefore bioenergetic and not only informational.

text.text: The second is a developmental account of the attachment prior (Tottenham and Vannucci, 2025).
text.formatted: The second is a developmental account of the attachment prior <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">(Tottenham and Vannucci, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: On this account, the prior is dyadic in construction and not merely acquired in a dyadic setting.
One partner generates the "need" term and the other supplies the "need metor-not-met term", so that neither is recoverable from either brain alone, and the unit of learning is the interaction itself.
We adopt this formulation for one specific implication: the quantity the two loops align around exists only across them, and is not two private quantities that happen to correlate.
Three further accounts have addressed the same dyad with related formalisms, and we distinguish our proposal from each.

Diaz-Rojas and colleagues (Diaz-Rojas et al., 2025) model parent-infant allostatic co-regulation in control-theoretic terms, treating the caregiver as a controller whose sensitivity and reaction speed determine how rapidly the infant returns towards a preferred state.
Sensitivity in their terms corresponds to a precision assignment in ours, and reaction speed to a property of policy selection.

Santaguida and colleagues (Santaguida et al., 2026) treat the infant-mother pair as a co-evolving dyadic system under active inference and derive the attachment styles from it, which is the closest formal precedent for the present proposal, although this system is pitched at the developmental origin of those styles rather than at the architecture that implements them.

text.text: And Tsubamoto & Horii (2026) model parent-infant co-regulation by combining a partially observable formulation of active interoceptive inference with a decentralised Bayesian account of communicative alignment.
text.formatted: And Tsubamoto & Horii (2026) model parent-infant co-regulation by combining a partially observable formulation of active interoceptive inference with a decentralised Bayesian account of communicative alignment.

text.text: Their asymmetry concerns access to the infant's visceral state, whereas ours concerns two systems with different activating conditions and terminations.

Furthermore, none of the above accounts is pitched at our level of organisation, which is the four NAMA modules and the two balances between them, re-described as components of one loop and the message passing that aligns them.
Nor does any of them extend beyond development, or treat the disrupted and disorganised cases specified in Section 3.4.
Two interacting brains are then two loops running concurrently (see That estimate is not symmetric, and it is here that the complementarity set out in Section 2.4 applies.

In the prototypical caregiving dyad, the child's loop runs the attachment system and the caregiver's loop the caregiving system, and the shared quantity is the estimate of whether the demand, signalled or anticipated, will be met.

In adult pair bonds, each partner runs both systems, and the roles alternate across episodes, which is one reason why paradigms that fix the roles for the duration of a measurement are more readily interpretable.
What is distributed across the dyad is regulatory work, but the partners do not perform the same work.
Costs and benefits therefore accrue asymmetrically and are ordinarily offset across repeated exchanges within an enduring relationship rather than within any single episode.
Whose cost is at issue must therefore be stated in each case, whether the recipient's, the caregiver's or the dyad's total, since a saving to the recipient may be offset by a cost to the caregiver.
Three consequences follow for the interpretation of synchrony.
First, synchrony is generated asymmetrically, so its magnitude does not disclose which partner's loop contributed the greater share (Section 4.2).
Second, the attachment and caregiving sides can, in principle, be characterised separately within the same dyad, and need not necessarily converge on a single dyadic value (Section 4.3).

Third, the cases on which our account bears most directly are those in which the two systems are mismatched (Section 4.5).  implications (Novembre et al., 2026; see also Burgess, 2013; Hakim et al., 2023; Holroyd, 2022).

text.text: Dependence can arise from common sensory input, shared task structure, arousal, movement, speech and turntaking as well as from reciprocity, so any reading of a measured value as reflecting an interpersonal mechanism is an inference beyond the measure.
In the following, we use synchrony for the measured dependence and avoid terms that imply a specific mechanism.

Synchrony has been interpreted in several ways that are not mutually exclusive: as entrainment to shared perceptual and communicative rhythms, as a signature of mutual prediction between interacting agents, as an index of emotion co-regulation, and as a correlate of interaction and relationship quality, (see e.g., De Felice et al., 2025; Feldman, 2017; Hasson et al., 2012; Hoehl et al., 2021; Kingsbury et al., 2019).

text.text: We propose an additional interpretation, which we state as a hypothesis.
On our account, INS and BBS may reflect, in part, where predictive and regulatory work is being invested within a dyad.
Under most conditions, this agrees with the interaction quality interpretation.
That said, predictive and regulatory work diverge under two conditions: where investment is high because regulation is failing, and where it is low because the available budget is depleted.
Both are considered in Section 4.4.
We stress at the outset that investment does not equal benefit.

Even where synchrony does reflect such work, it records that work is being expended, not the state it is expended towards, and the remainder of this section should be read with that distinction in view.
Two of these interpretations, mutual prediction and emotion co-regulation, correspond to components of the loop.

Mutual prediction is located primarily in the mental state representation module, since predicting an attachment figure's conduct requires a generative model of another agent's hidden states (Lehmann et al., 2024).

text.text: Emotion co-regulation is located predominantly in the emotion regulation module.
Across a dyad, it is the allostatic correction performed jointly: one partner supplies, through their own action, the conditions the other's model predicts will restore the regulated state.
The two are not independent, since a correction cannot be delivered by a partner who cannot predict when it is needed.
Mutual prediction is therefore a precondition for co-regulation rather than a parallel mechanism.

This priority accords with the definition of parental sensitivity, in which the perception and interpretation of the infant's signals precede a prompt and appropriate response (Ainsworth et al., 1978), and with the meta-analytic finding that parental mentalisation predicts attachment security in part through sensitivity (Zeegers et al., 2017).

text.text: Where the attachment figure is at once the source of threat and the figure to whom proximity would be sought, the attachment system may remain strongly engaged while physiological regulation is impaired (Graf et al., 2022).

text.text: And the dyad may become tightly coordinated around the wrong target, namely the monitoring of threat, the management of the caregiver's state, and/or the maintenance of proximity despite fear.

It is instructive that mutual prediction can be fully achieved under these conditions: a child may come to anticipate a caregiver's anger with considerable accuracy while remaining oriented to danger rather than regulated towards safety.
Predictability is therefore not sufficient for co-regulation.
Where care is instead reliably absent, no such coordination is established, and the expected signature is the failure of synchronisation rather than its misdirection.
We would accordingly expect the two routes to be dissociable in the form of the synchrony and not in its magnitude alone.

A design comparing romantic partners with strangers does not assess attachment quality per se, but it is not thereby uninformative about attachment, since child-parent relationships and romantic partnerships are attachment bonds in the technical sense.
